claims.text: The quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are equiatomic and single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
Local chemical short-range order in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni produces an optimized distribution of stacking-fault energies.
The stacking-fault-energy distribution in the quinary alloy enables balanced activation of dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
The quaternary and ternary subsets develop less uniform local chemical environments than the quinary alloy.
Less uniform chemical environments in the quaternary and ternary subsets produce different or less optimal stacking-fault-energy distributions.
The quaternary and ternary subsets have reduced deformation-twin activity relative to the quinary alloy.
Differences in dislocation-slip and twinning activity cause differences in work hardening and resistance to localized failure.
Local chemical short-range order modulates the stacking-fault-energy landscape.
A more uniform stacking-fault-energy landscape in the quinary alloy promotes combined dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
Combined dislocation glide and twinning produce higher strain-hardening rates in the quinary alloy.
Reduced constituent count in the quaternary and ternary subsets is associated with lower twin density and a diminished balance between deformation mechanisms.
The diminished balance between slip and twinning affects ductility and failure resistance.
The quinary alloy will exhibit higher deformation-twin density than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The quinary alloy will exhibit a higher strain-hardening rate than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The quinary alloy will exhibit greater tensile ductility than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The superior mechanical properties assigned to the quinary baseline arise from optimized internal chemical order.

The proposed mechanism applies under ambient-temperature, moderate-strain-rate deformation of identically processed, single-phase FCC alloys whose behavior is dominated by dislocation glide and twinning.
